text: auditd, the Linux Audit Daemon, works at the kernel layer rather than the application layer. Application logs only record what the software itself was coded to mention. auditd watches system calls and file access directly, based on rules you configure, and logs matching events to audit.log regardless of whether any program chose to log them. That's the real distinction between the two kinds of logging.

A watch rule tells the kernel what to track: auditctl -w /etc/shadow -p wa -k shadow_changes watches that path for write and attribute changes, tagging matching entries with a searchable key. Rules added with auditctl directly vanish on reboot, though — for a rule that needs to survive a restart, it goes into a file under /etc/audit/rules.d/, loaded automatically at startup.

Put the pieces together and you get the full pipeline: a rule gets set, either at runtime or as a persistent file. The kernel logs any matching syscall or file access to audit.log. From there, ausearch filters for specific events by key, file, user, or time, while aureport gives a faster summarized view across a whole category before you drill into specifics.

ausearch -k shadow_changes or ausearch -f /etc/shadow pulls the exact matching events for that rule, down to the timestamp, the process, and the user ID involved. aureport -au summarizes authentication activity across the whole system; aureport -f summarizes file access the same way. Checking the summary report first, then filtering down with ausearch once something looks worth investigating, is usually the faster order to work in during a real investigation.

That's what makes auditd catch what an application log can't: a text editor used to modify /etc/shadow never logs anything about that file specifically, but the watch rule fires at the kernel level regardless, capturing exactly who changed it and when.
